basis: two loves; earthly and heavenly cities
note: Augustine's two cities arise from love of self to contempt of God or love of God to contempt of self, an interpretive framework for the commentary's proud earthly height and Godward orientation.

basis: thanksgiving for the holy name in prayer
note: The commentary’s remembered and praised name is a liturgical act; the post-meal prayer thanks the holy Father for his holy name made to dwell in believers’ hearts.
The Didache directs Christians to pray the Lord's Prayer three times daily, preserving “hallowed be your name” as a repeated discipline of name-sanctification.

The letter describes Christians as passing their days on earth while holding citizenship in heaven, an early Christian interpretation of the vertical choice between present life and a higher homeland.
Ignatius rejects corruptible food and the pleasures of this life in favor of God, a concrete early Christian appropriation of preferring what is lasting.

basis: Mary’s “magnifying” as the soul’s reception of God
note: The commentary says the name raises the named one’s remembrance; Origen’s homily on Mary’s Magnificat explains her soul’s magnifying of the Lord as a change in the human recipient’s capacity to perceive and receive God, not an increase in God’s greatness.
Origen treats “hallowed be your name” as a petition about God's name being sanctified in those who pray, extending the commentary's verbal glorification into moral practice.
The present form of this world is passing away, a concise counterpart to the commentary's judgment that the selected worldly life is lower and nonlasting.

basis: the world passes, God’s will abides
note: The commentary hears al-dunya as the nearer, lesser life; John contrasts the passing world and its desires with the one who does God’s will and abides forever.
The world and its desire pass away while the one doing God's will remains forever, closely matching the commentary's present-life versus enduring-good contrast.
The commentary contrasts the proud ruler with the lowly life; Peter tells believers to humble themselves under God’s mighty hand so he may exalt them at the proper time.
The commentary links divine majesty and light with the great fire; Paul describes God as dwelling in unapproachable light and as the one to whom honor and eternal dominion belong.

basis: rich not haughty or hopeful in wealth
note: The rich are not to be haughty or set hope on uncertain wealth, explicitly connecting worldly possession with the pride that the commentary treats as fallen height.

basis: visible transient things and unseen eternal things
note: The commentary hears al-dunya as the nearer, lesser life and the surah contrasts it with what lasts; Paul says visible things are temporary while unseen things are eternal.
Paul contrasts visible things that are temporary with unseen things that are eternal, closely framing the commentary's choice between the near life and what endures.

basis: God’s glory shines in Christ’s face
note: The commentary’s gloss joins radiance and light to the Lord’s face; Paul describes the knowledge of God’s glory in the face of Christ, with light shining in human hearts.
The Lord's revelation in flaming fire brings retribution on those who do not know or obey God, making divine judgment rather than mere physical flame the point of the fire.

basis: self-exalting claimant who declares himself God
note: The lawless figure exalts himself against every god and declares himself God, a focused Christian counter-picture to Pharaoh's “most high lord” claim.

The commentary says Moses’ magicians believe and receive high degrees; Paul names Jannes and Jambres as opponents of Moses who resist the truth, preserving a contrary Christian memory of the magicians.
The letter names Jannes and Jambres as opponents of Moses, preserving a Christian interpretive identification for the Egyptian-magician contest developed in the commentary.

basis: Herod takes glory and is struck
note: Herod accepts a divine acclamation instead of giving God glory and is struck down, a concrete Christian royal warning against usurped greatness.

basis: servants of the Most High amid divination
note: A divining slave calls Paul and companions servants of the Most High God; its setting makes a Christian comparison for the commentary's contest between revelation and magical power.

basis: Creator not dwelling in handmade shrines
note: Paul calls God maker of world and heaven and says he does not dwell in hand-made sanctuaries, a distinct Christian qualification of elevated worship-houses.

basis: Most High not in handmade houses
note: Stephen says the Most High does not dwell in handmade houses, an interpretive tension with the commentary's raised houses: the Name may be worshiped there without containing the Most High.

basis: set the mind above, not on earth
note: The commentary sets the high against the near earthly life; Paul commands believers to seek the things above rather than things on earth, stating that orientation directly.
Paul commands a mind set on things above rather than earthly things, an unusually direct verbalized high/low orientation.
The exalted Christ is above every rule, authority, power, dominion, and every name named, using height and naming together to deny final status to worldly powers.
The Son sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high after making purification, a concentrated heavenly-height image that joins exaltation to cleansing rather than arrogance.
The faithful desire a better, heavenly country, an exact directional alternative to giving preference to the nearer worldly life.
The commentary places Moses’ story beside the warning against choosing the near life; Hebrews says Moses chose mistreatment with God’s people over the temporary pleasure of sin.

basis: Moses values reward above Egypt’s wealth
note: The commentary’s low-life choice is a question of value; Hebrews says Moses considered reproach greater wealth than Egypt’s treasures because he looked to the reward.

basis: God as consuming fire in a call to worship
note: The commentary links divine majesty and the great fire; Hebrews urges reverent worship because God is a consuming fire, bringing the image into a Christian liturgical warning.
Believers have no lasting city here but seek the one to come, a concise Christian analogue to rejecting the nearer life for what abides.

basis: praise and confession of the name
note: The commentary places remembrance of the Lord’s name before prayer; Hebrews describes continual praise as a sacrifice of lips that confess God’s name.
Believers continually offer praise to God as lips confess his name, closely paralleling the commentary's remembered name expressed in worship.
The Son proclaims God's name among brothers and sings praise in the assembly, a communal form of naming and glorifying God.

basis: Melchizedek priest of God Most High
note: Hebrews receives Genesis 14's priest of God Most High into a Christian priestly argument, making the older high-title tradition an explicit interpretive resource.

basis: humility before the Lord brings exaltation
note: The commentary makes height and lowliness an axis; James commands readers to humble themselves before the Lord, who will exalt them.
Jesus contrasts loving one's life in this world with keeping it for eternal life, directly matching the commentary's choice between the near life and what endures.
The commentary’s command to raise the Lord’s name is echoed when Jesus prays that the Father glorify his name; the heavenly voice answers that it has been glorified and will be glorified again.

basis: ask in Jesus' name; Father glorified
note: Prayer in Jesus' name is ordered to the Father's glorification, explicitly joining name, prayer, and divine honor as 87:15 does.
Jesus says he manifested the Father's name to those given him, a New Testament development of the commentary's claim that a name discloses the one named.

basis: worship not bound to mountain or Jerusalem
note: Jesus anticipates worship no longer bound to a particular mountain or Jerusalem, offering a Christian reframing of elevation and sacred place.

basis: human glory versus glory from God
note: Jesus contrasts receiving glory from one another with seeking glory from the only God, making human honor a rival to true divine recognition.

basis: Son of the Most High; royal throne
note: Gabriel calls Jesus Son of the Most High and promises David's throne, setting a divinely granted royal title beside Pharaoh's falsely appropriated highest lordship.
The commentary links the Lord’s name and remembered honor to elevation; Mary’s prayer begins by magnifying the Lord, a direct worship formula from a lowly speaker.
The commentary’s tasbih declares God free of defect and exalts his name; Mary says the Mighty One has done great things for her and holy is his name.
Mary calls the Mighty One's deeds great and his name holy, continuing the name-and-greatness language beside the later reversal of the mighty and lowly in the same song.
The commentary treats Pharaoh’s claim to highest rank as arrogance; Mary’s hymn says God scatters the proud in the intention of their hearts, adding the divine reversal of self-exaltation.
The commentary pairs a self-exalting ruler with the low/near life; Mary’s hymn says God brings rulers down from thrones and exalts the lowly, a direct reversal of claimed human height.
Mary's song brings down the mighty from thrones and exalts the lowly, making the commentary's high/low axis a narrative reversal.

The commentary sets true divine height against a creature’s arrogant claim; Jesus says he saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning, a specific heavenly fall that resonates with the descent of Isaiah’s self-exalting figure.
The angelic hymn places glory “in the highest,” a concise heavenly response to the commentary's opening Most High and its account of a revelation-bearer.

basis: trying to save life and losing it
note: The commentary warns that people prefer the low, near life; Jesus says whoever seeks to save life will lose it, while whoever loses life for his sake will save it.

basis: gaining the world and losing one’s life
note: The commentary criticizes preferring the low, near life; Jesus asks what it profits someone to gain the whole world and forfeit life, making the choice’s cost explicit.
Jesus' Gehenna citation describes an unquenched fire and an undying worm, a close comparison for the continuing punitive condition surrounding 87:12–13.
The question of gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life gives a sharp ethical measure for the commentary's preference of worldly life.
The commentary calls Pharaoh’s highest-lord claim arrogance; Jesus says the one who exalts himself will be humbled and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.
The commentary names the great fire as the wretched person’s end; Jesus’ judgment scene sends the accursed into eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.
The judgment scene sends the cursed to eternal fire, a direct eschatological counterpart to the commentary's greatest fire.
The commentary says people prefer the near, lower life; Jesus warns against storing treasure on earth, where moth and rust destroy, giving the choice a concrete object and cost.
Jesus forbids storing treasure on earth because it decays and is stolen, concretizing why a life preferred as “lower” cannot be the final good.
Against the commentary’s preference for the near life, Jesus directs disciples to store treasure in heaven, where it cannot be destroyed, supplying the alternative value.

basis: treasure in heaven does not decay
note: The complementary command locates uncorruptible treasure in heaven, supplying the durable upward alternative to present-world preference.
The commentary says people choose the low and near life; Jesus says the heart follows its treasure, making the preference for earthly life an inward allegiance rather than a mere circumstance.
The commentary names a choice of the lower, nearer life; Jesus says no one can serve both God and mammon, making that preference a direct choice of master.

basis: prayer that the Father’s name be hallowed
note: The commentary’s opening command is praise of the Lord’s name; Jesus’ prayer begins by asking that the Father’s name be hallowed, placing sanctification of the name inside communal prayer.
Jesus teaches prayer beginning with the sanctification of the Father's name, a direct Christian liturgical counterpart to glorifying the Lord's name.

basis: every knee bows at the name
note: The commentary’s name-and-prayer pairing becomes embodied worship here: at Jesus’ name every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth is to bow.
The commentary joins remembering the Lord’s name to prayer; Paul says every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord to the glory of God the Father.

basis: confession brings glory to the Father
note: The confession of Jesus as Lord is “to the glory of God the Father,” giving an explicitly verbal act of honoring God beside the commentary's name-praise.

basis: exalted and given the name above every name
note: The commentary says the Lord’s name is raised and honored; Paul says God highly exalted Jesus and bestowed the name above every name, locating exaltation in the Christ hymn.

basis: God highly exalts and grants the name
note: After Christ's self-humbling, God highly exalts him and gives the name above every name, setting bestowed elevation against self-claimed greatness.

basis: earthly-mindedness as the road to destruction
note: The commentary calls the chosen earthly life low and nearer; Paul describes people whose minds are set on earthly things and whose end is destruction, supplying a concrete moral consequence.
Those whose end is destruction set their minds on earthly things, a New Testament diagnosis of the orientation the commentary calls preference for the lower life.
The commentary’s axis contrasts the near life with a higher enduring orientation; Paul says believers’ citizenship is in heaven, naming the alternative to earthly-mindedness.
The following verse supplies the opposing allegiance, citizenship in heaven, so the spatial axis becomes a communal identity rather than an abstraction.
The beast opens its mouth to blaspheme God and his name, the explicit opposite of the commentary's command to sanctify and glorify the divine name.
The commentary links tasbih, majesty, and the Lord’s name; Revelation asks who will not fear and glorify God’s name, then says he alone is holy and nations will worship.

basis: glorify God's name because he is holy
note: The heavenly song asks who will not glorify God's name, for he alone is holy; it fuses name-praise with the holiness content of tasbih.
Babylon glorifies herself, lives luxuriously, and claims secure queenship; this is a concentrated apocalyptic portrait of proud height joined to worldly preference.

basis: lake of fire called second death
note: Revelation calls the lake of fire the second death, a Christian way of naming final fiery loss beside 87:12–13's paradoxical life/death condition.

basis: God's face and name on servants
note: The final servants see God's face and bear his name on their foreheads, a concentrated Christian pairing of the commentary's sought divine face and remembered name.
The living creatures' continual “holy, holy, holy” before the enthroned Almighty offers a Christian heavenly analogue to transcendent praise.
Paul makes calling on the Lord's name the saving response, a direct Christian use of divine naming as invocation rather than self-honor.

basis: Paul reads Pharaoh’s role as serving God’s name
note: The commentary presents Pharaoh’s “highest lord” claim as false human elevation; Paul quotes Exodus to say Pharaoh was raised up so God’s power and name would be proclaimed, interpreting the same ruler as an instrument of divine sovereignty.
Tertullian explains the opening prayer petition as asking that God's name be held holy in us, interpreting name-sanctification as lived conduct as well as speech.

basis: throne glory, streams of fire, and unapproachable face
note: The commentary’s gloss connects the Lord’s facial radiance and majesty with light and fire; Enoch’s heavenly throne vision joins fiery streams to overwhelming glory and a face no flesh can behold.

basis: worship and glorification of the Lord of Spirits’ name
note: The commentary joins the Lord’s name to praise and highness; 1 Enoch pictures earth’s inhabitants falling down to worship and bless, glorify, and celebrate the name of the Lord of Spirits.
Mattathias warns that the sinner's glory ends in worms and shame; it makes worldly exaltation transient and degradable.
The stricken king who had thought himself superhuman recognizes that he is mortal, a close royal counter-story to Pharaoh-like claims of supreme height.

basis: Babel’s tower as rebellion against God
note: The commentary treats a creature’s claim to height as arrogant usurpation; Genesis Rabbah reads the tower builders’ ascent as rebellion against heaven, making the biblical tower more than an architectural project.
Josephus interprets the tower builders as seeking security and defiance rather than gratitude to God; this intensifies Gen 11's self-raised name in the commentary's terms.
The Kaddish opens by asking that God's great name be magnified and sanctified, an enduring Jewish liturgical interpretation of praise as elevation of the Name.

basis: this world as a vestibule to the world to come
note: The commentary hears al-dunya as the lower and nearer life that people choose; Avot calls this world a vestibule before the world to come and urges preparation for entry into the latter.

basis: relative worth of the two worlds
note: The commentary’s choice of the nearer life is a value judgment; Avot says one hour of good deeds in this world is better than the whole world to come, yet one hour of serenity in the world to come is better than all this world, preserving both sides of the contrast.
Rabbi Levitas' injunction to be very, very humble supplies a terse Jewish ethical counterweight to the commentary's ruler who turns height into pride.
The moon-testimony procedures ask witnesses about the new crescent's position, height, direction, and form, a concrete Jewish reading-world for the commentary's discerned crescent above the horizon.
The Mishnah distinguishes the Temple's pronunciation of the Name from its substitute outside, giving ritual precision to the commentary's house, name, and worship nexus.

basis: magnifying and sanctifying the great name
note: The commentary commands praise of the Lord’s high name; the Qaddish opens with a prayer that God’s great name be magnified and sanctified in the world he created.

basis: pride begins by leaving the Lord
note: Sirach defines human pride as departure from the Lord, directly interpreting the commentary's self-raised ruler as a theological, not merely social, failure.
David ascribes greatness, glory, and all that is in heaven and earth to YHWH, who is exalted as head above all; it is a comprehensive scriptural form of the commentary's vertical praise.
Even while Solomon prays about the name-bearing house, he says the highest heaven cannot contain God; this qualifies a merely spatial reading of raised worship-houses.
The commentary cites houses raised for worship where the Lord’s name is mentioned; Solomon calls the temple the place where God said his name would be, tying a worship house to the indwelling name.

basis: house where God's name is; prayer
note: Solomon asks God to attend to the house of which he said “My name shall be there” and to the prayer toward it, closely pairing house, name, and prayer.

The commentary pairs the Lord’s exaltation with a worshipper’s prayer; Hannah says her strength is exalted in the Lord and rejoices in his salvation, placing elevation in grateful devotion rather than self-claim.

basis: God brings low and raises up
note: The commentary makes highness and lowliness opposite ends of one axis; Hannah’s prayer says the Lord makes poor and rich and brings low and raises up.

basis: God brings low and lifts up
note: Hannah's hymn says that YHWH makes poor and rich, brings low and also lifts up; it gives the commentary's vertical axis a divine reversal in human status.

basis: the needy raised from dust to sit with princes
note: The commentary describes the chosen life as low and lesser; Hannah says God lifts the needy from the dust and seats them with princes, a concrete reversal of low status.
The people called by God's name must humble themselves, pray, and seek his face; this joins named belonging, prayer, and the reversal of proud elevation.

basis: blessed name, kings raised and removed
note: The commentary contrasts God’s true height with a ruler’s claim; Daniel blesses God’s name forever because wisdom and might belong to him and he removes and sets up kings.

The commentary labels سَبِّحِ as tasbih, glorifying God; Daniel thanks and praises the God of his fathers for revealing the king’s secret, using the Aramaic praise cognate in a prayer that credits divine wisdom.
Nebuchadnezzar calls the rescued men servants of the Most High God at the mouth of the furnace, holding the high divine title and a decisive fire in one scene.
Daniel's Aramaic עִלָּיָא, used for God beside the furnace, is a cognate witness for the high-title language developed around ٱلْأَعْلَى.

basis: worship under threat of the furnace
note: The commentary joins praise of the Lord’s high name to the great fire; after the three Judeans survive Nebuchadnezzar’s blazing furnace, the king blesses their God because they refused to worship any god but him.
After deliverance from the furnace, Nebuchadnezzar blesses the God of the servants; the fire becomes a scene of divine praise rather than the final fate of the wicked.

The commentary’s Pharaoh claims supreme rule for himself; the heavenly decree in Daniel says the Most High rules the kingdom of humanity and gives it to whom he wills, framing Nebuchadnezzar’s later boast and humbling.

basis: king boasts of his own majesty
note: The commentary identifies Pharaoh’s “highest lord” claim as arrogant self-exaltation; Nebuchadnezzar claims Babylon was built by his own power for the glory of his majesty, making the ruler’s boast explicit.

basis: kingdom taken during the king’s boast
note: The commentary presents Pharaoh’s “I am the highest lord” as a creature’s false claim; Daniel’s heavenly voice interrupts Nebuchadnezzar’s boast and announces that his kingship has departed from him.

basis: Aramaic title for the Most High
note: The commentary labels ٱلْأَعْلَى with an elevation root; after his humiliation Nebuchadnezzar blesses the Aramaic “Most High” and praises his everlasting dominion, coupling a related Semitic title with worship.
The commentary opposes God’s true highness to a creature’s arrogance; Nebuchadnezzar honors the King of heaven and concludes that those who walk in pride God is able to humble.
Nebuchadnezzar's heart is lifted up and he is deposed from royal throne, a royal narrative of self-exaltation turned into abasement.

basis: Belshazzar lifts himself against heaven's Lord
note: Belshazzar exalts himself against the Lord of heaven and fails to glorify the God who holds his breath, closely matching the commentary's opposition between claimed greatness and divine praise.

basis: place for God's name to dwell
note: The chosen worship site is where YHWH makes his name dwell, providing a Torah antecedent for the commentary's raised houses where the name is remembered.

basis: chosen sanctuary where God places his name
note: The commentary cites houses authorized for worship with the Lord’s name in them; Deuteronomy commands Israel to seek the place God chooses for his name and dwelling, supplying the covenant sanctuary background.
Moses announces that he will proclaim YHWH's name and calls hearers to ascribe greatness to God, a close Torah parallel to name-praise and takbir.
The commentary names the great fire in the judgment scene; Moses warns Israel that the Lord their God is a consuming fire, so the fire image also expresses divine holiness and judgment.

The commentary treats Pharaoh’s self-ascribed height as arrogance; Moses warns Israel against saying “my power and the might of my hand” made its wealth, a specific warning against taking divine provision as one’s own greatness.
The warning against saying “my power” gained wealth isolates the self-crediting impulse that accompanies the commentary's preference for worldly life and corrupt greatness.

basis: Moses sings YHWH's exaltation over Pharaoh
note: Moses' victory song calls YHWH highly exalted after horse and rider are thrown into the sea, directly joining the Moses-Pharaoh setting with rightful divine height.
The commentary defines tasbih as declaring God free of evil and cites divine majesty; Moses’ song asks who is like the Lord, majestic in holiness and awesome in deeds.
The song asks who is like YHWH, majestic in holiness and awesome in praises, giving concrete Mosaic language for the commentary's tasbih as transcendence and majesty.
The commentary’s command to glorify the Lord’s name is matched by Moses’ song, which calls the Lord “my God” and says he will praise and exalt him after the sea deliverance.
Jethro confesses YHWH greater than all gods precisely in the affair where Egyptians acted presumptuously, pairing divine greatness with the undoing of proud power.
YHWH calls Moses to Sinai's summit and Moses goes up, giving a concrete sacred scene for upward call, divine height, and revelation.
The commentary links remembering the Lord’s name with prayer; God says he will come and bless at every altar where he causes his name to be remembered, joining invocation to sacrifice.
At an altar, God promises to come and bless wherever he causes his name to be remembered; this is a spatial worship counterpart to remembering the Lord's name and praying.
The command to Moses and the elders, “Come up to YHWH,” realizes the commentary's observation that an invitation to come can be a summons toward a height.

basis: glory appearing as devouring fire on the mountain
note: The commentary connects divine majesty and light with the great fire; at Sinai the Lord’s glory appears to Israel like a devouring fire on the mountain’s summit, joining height, glory, and fire.

The commentary links remembrance to the Lord’s name; God identifies himself to Moses and says this name is his memorial through all generations, using the Hebrew z-k-r family for enduring remembrance.
God calls YHWH his name forever and his memorial through generations, directly pairing the divine name with remembrance as 87:15 does.
God's זִכְרִי, “memorial,” is a Hebrew cognate of the commentary's ذِكْر; the verse makes it inseparable from the revealed divine name.
The verse's שֵׁם, God's enduring name, provides an actual Hebrew cognate comparison for the commentary's ٱسْم rather than a root-label inference.
Moses hides his face because he fears to look at God, giving a biblical fear scene for the commentary's frightened Moses before divine reassurance.

basis: seeing God’s face and the limit of mortal life
note: The commentary cites language about the Lord’s face as overwhelming glory and light; when Moses asks to see God’s glory, Exodus says no human can see God’s face and live, setting a distinct boundary around that face imagery.

basis: the Lord descends and proclaims his name
note: The commentary calls for praise of the Lord’s name; at Sinai the Lord descends in a cloud and proclaims the divine name before Moses, giving the naming formula a theophanic setting.
The commentary defines tasbih as denying every evil of God; the proclamation following the name calls the Lord merciful, gracious, patient, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.

The commentary quotes Pharaoh’s direct claim to be the highest lord; Exodus instead has Pharaoh deny knowing YHWH and refuse obedience, preserving a distinct biblical portrayal of the same ruler’s resistance.
Exodus portrays Pharaoh answering “Who is YHWH?” and refusing obedience; beside the commentary's Pharaoh who claims the highest lordship, this is a rival account of his rejection of the true Lord.
Pharaoh calls wise men, sorcerers, and Egyptian magicians, the biblical counterpart to the commentary's Moses-and-magicians scene.
Aaron's staff swallows the magicians' staffs, a narrative precedent for the claim that Moses will be superior in a contest with magic.

basis: magicians recognize God’s act but are not converted
note: The commentary notes that Moses’ magicians believe and receive high degrees; Exodus has Pharaoh’s magicians admit “the finger of God” but remain in the confrontation, without the conversion and reward narrated in the Qur’anic scene.

The commentary’s Pharaoh claims the highest rank for himself; God tells the biblical Pharaoh he has been kept standing so divine power may be shown and God’s name proclaimed throughout the earth, reversing the claim.
God charges Pharaoh with still exalting himself against the people, a direct biblical instance of the commentary's warning that earthly height becomes arrogant tyranny.
The Tyrian ruler's heart becomes proud because of his splendor and he is cast to the ground, a vivid vertical reversal for corrupted height.
The same ruler's profanation brings fire from his midst to consume him; it joins arrogant elevation and punitive fire without treating divine glory itself as evil.

The commentary’s Pharaoh appropriates the Lord’s highest title; Ezekiel addresses Tyre’s ruler as a man who says “I am a god” while sitting in a godlike seat, another ruler’s false claim to divine rank.
God vindicates and sanctifies his great name after its profanation; this supplies a public, historical dimension to the commentary's divine-name praise.

basis: a tower reaching heaven and a self-made name
note: The commentary contrasts the Lord’s high name with a ruler’s false elevation; Babel’s builders seek a name for themselves while building a tower toward heaven, joining self-exaltation and name-making in one scene.

basis: Hebrew shem and Arabic ism in the self-made name
note: The commentary labels ٱسْمَ as a name whose mention is raised; Babel’s builders seek to make a shem for themselves while raising a tower toward heaven. Hebrew shem is cognate with Arabic ism, though the Hebrew verse does not derive it from height.

basis: make a name; tower to heaven
note: Babel's builders say “make a name for ourselves” while raising a tower toward heaven, a deliberate human self-elevation that reverses glorification of the Most High's name.

The commentary’s high/low axis includes a creature’s attempt to rise; after Babel’s tower project, God scatters the builders and the city is left unfinished, a narrative reversal of their ascent and self-made name.
God, rather than Abram, promises to make Abram's name great; this distinguishes bestowed honorable remembrance from the self-made name of Babel and Pharaoh-like pride.

basis: El Elyon; creator heaven and earth
note: Melchizedek blesses Abram by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth; it supplies a biblical divine title whose height belongs to the Creator.
The Hebrew title עֶלְיוֹן (Most High) is a cognate comparison for the commentary's ٱلْأَعْلَى, and Gen 14 uses it of the Creator rather than an exalted ruler.

The commentary’s “Most High” language has a Hebrew counterpart in Melchizedek’s blessing of God as ʿelyon; the verse blesses that God for delivering Abram’s enemies, joining the title to praise and sovereignty.

basis: go up; build house; God glorified
note: The command to go up the mountain, bring wood, and build God's house joins the commentary's upward summons to a house whose purpose is divine glorification.

basis: call on and proclaim the exalted name
note: The commentary’s command to praise the high name is matched by Isaiah’s thanksgiving instruction to call on the Lord’s name and proclaim among the nations that it is exalted.

The commentary develops a silhouette rising above the horizon and a ruler’s claimed height; Isaiah addresses a fallen morning star before recounting the speaker’s ascent and boast, adding a celestial image to the self-exaltation scene.

basis: “I will make myself like the Most High”
note: The commentary cites Pharaoh claiming “I am your Lord Most High”; the taunting king in Isaiah explicitly resolves to make himself like the Most High, exposing the same creaturely seizure of divine height.

basis: aspiring to likeness of the Most High
note: The taunt's arrogant ruler plans to ascend above clouds and make himself like the Most High; its counter-claim clarifies why a creature's use of supreme height is corrupt.
The commentary says a king’s rising can mean tyranny and arrogance; Isaiah’s self-exalting figure is brought down to Sheol, supplying the reversal implicit in the Qur’anic judgment on Pharaoh.

basis: human pride lowered, Lord alone exalted
note: The commentary makes height reversible when a ruler exalts himself; Isaiah says the proud eyes of humanity will be brought low and YHWH alone exalted.
Isaiah says haughty human eyes will be brought low and YHWH alone exalted, making the commentary's high/low axis a judgment on rival elevation.
Isaiah's latter-days vision establishes the mountain of YHWH's house as highest among mountains, a spatial counterpart to the commentary's raised houses for divine remembrance.

basis: come; go up to YHWH's house
note: Nations say “Come, let us go up” to YHWH's house for instruction, combining the commentary's upward invitation with a worshiping community.

basis: exaltation and praise of the name
note: The commentary links tasbih with raising the Lord’s name; Isaiah says “I will exalt you” and praise the Lord’s name for faithful wonders, giving that pairing a worship context.
Isaiah says that YHWH's name and memorial are the soul's desire, making remembered divine naming an act of directed longing rather than mere recollection.
Topheth is prepared deep and wide for the king, with abundant wood kindled by YHWH; it gives the commentary's great fire a royal-judgment analogue.

basis: lift eyes on high; Creator of stars
note: Isaiah commands hearers to lift their eyes on high and see the creator who brings out the starry host, furnishing a biblical celestial counterpart to the high-horizon imagery.
YHWH says that this is his name and that he gives his glory to no other; it directly answers the commentary's creaturely seizure of divine-high status.
God grants faithful outsiders an everlasting name better than sons and daughters, making elevated naming a divine gift that outlasts ordinary earthly continuance.

The commentary sets the Lord’s highness against the low, near life and a ruler’s vaunted height; Isaiah calls God the High and Lofty One who also dwells with the contrite and lowly, redefining true elevation.
The one dwelling in the high and holy place says his name is Holy, binding the commentary's two opening poles, height and divine naming, in one prophetic declaration.

basis: glory to God's Name, not ourselves

basis: God raises the humble and casts down the wicked

basis: name exalted above earth and heaven

basis: name exalted above earth and heaven

basis: remembering the Lord’s name against worldly reliance

basis: prayer for the light of God’s face

basis: remembered royal name and enduring praise

basis: Most High; great king over earth

basis: God puts one down and lifts another

basis: majestic name and glory above the heavens

basis: Hebrew shem and Arabic ism in praise

basis: glory due the name and offerings in the courts

basis: one king over earth and one name

basis: profit of arrogance and boastful wealth
